chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mansur ibn Yunus, from Abu al-Ma'mun al-Harithi, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'What is the right of the believer upon the believer?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Among the rights of the believer upon the believer is affection for him in his chest, and sharing in his wealth, and taking care of his family in his absence, and helping him against whoever oppresses him, and if there were spoils distributed among the Muslims and he was absent, to take his share for him, and when he dies, to visit his grave.'

And that he should not oppress him, and not deceive him, and not betray him, and not abandon him, and not belittle him, and not say 'Uff' to him. And if he says 'Uff' to him, then there is no Wilayah (bond of affinity) between them. And if he says to him, 'You are my enemy,' then one of the two has disbelieved. And if he suspects him, faith dissolves in his heart just as salt dissolves in water.

key_terms.أُفٍّ: An expression of slight annoyance or contempt
key_terms.الْخَلَفَ: Taking care of or standing in for (specifically regarding family)
key_terms.الْمَوَدَّةَ: Affection or love in the heart
key_terms.الْوَلَايَة: Bond of affinity, guardianship, or close relationship

ai.seo_question: What are the specific rights and duties of a believer towards another believer in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: In this foundational hadith from Al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) delineates the comprehensive rights of a believer upon their brother, extending beyond mere social courtesy to include deep emotional affinity (mawaddah), financial solidarity, and active defense against oppression. The text underscores the fragility of faith, using the metaphor of salt dissolving in water to illustrate how suspicion erodes iman, while declaring that a specific utterance ('anta aduwwi') can signify a rupture in spiritual brotherhood. This narration serves as a cornerstone for understanding the concept of 'wilayah' (spiritual affinity) in Shia jurisprudence, linking interpersonal ethics directly to the preservation of one's faith.
